title: Who were the “sons of God” who took the daughters of men?
summary: Genesis 6 says the sons of God took wives from the daughters of men and that children were born to them, just before the Lord resolves to destroy man. The passage does not say who the sons of God were.
text: KJV Genesis 6:1: “when men began to multiply on the face of the earth, and daughters were born unto them”. KJV 6:2: “That the sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair; and they took them wives of all which they chose.” Hebrew (WLC) 6:2: וַיִּרְא֤וּ בְנֵי־הָֽאֱלֹהִים֙ אֶת־בְּנֹ֣ות הָֽאָדָ֔ם [and the sons of God saw the daughters of man]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 6:2: Ἰδόντες δὲ υἱοὶ τοῦ Θεοῦ τὰς θυγατέρας τῶν ἀνθρώπων [and the sons of God, having seen the daughters of men]. KJV 6:4: “There were giants in the earth in those days; and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare children to them, the same became mighty men which were of old, men of renown.” Hebrew (WLC) 6:4: הַנְּפִלִ֞ים הָי֣וּ בָאָרֶץ֮ בַּיָּמִ֣ים הָהֵם֒ [the Nephilim were in the earth in those days]. Brenton Greek 6:4: Οἱ δὲ γίγαντες ἦσαν ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς ἐν ταῖς ἡμέραις ἐκείναις [and the giants were on the earth in those days]. KJV 6:5: “And God saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth”. KJV Job 1:6: “Now there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before the Lord, and Satan came also among them.” Hebrew (WLC) Job 1:6: וַיָּבֹ֙אוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י הָאֱלֹהִ֔ים [and the sons of God came]. Brenton Greek Job 1:6: ἦλθον οἱ ἄγγελοι τοῦ Θεοῦ [the angels of God came]. KJV Job 38:7: “and all the sons of God shouted for joy”. KJV Matthew 22:30: “they neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven”. KJV Jude 1:6: “the angels which kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation”. KJV 2 Peter 2:4: “God spared not the angels that sinned”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/6/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN06.htm; https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/18/1/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JOB01.htm.
reasoning: The passage sets two groups beside each other, the sons of God and the daughters of men, and tells of their marriages and children immediately before God sees that the wickedness of man is great. Nothing earlier in Genesis uses the phrase “sons of God”, and the passage does not explain it. Verse 4 also leaves open how the giants are related to these unions: it says they were in the earth in those days, and also after that, when the sons of God came in to the daughters of men, without saying that the giants were the children. In the Hebrew edition quoted, the two words for “sons of God” in Genesis 6:2 are the same two words as in Job 1:6, where the sons of God present themselves before the Lord. Brenton’s Greek has “sons of God” in Genesis 6 and “angels of God” in Job 1:6.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readers have identified the sons of God as heavenly beings, as men of one family line marrying women of another, or as rulers. Each is an interpretation; the passage states none of them, and this record asserts none. The same Hebrew words in Job show that the phrase is shared; shared wording does not settle what it means in Genesis 6. Jude 1:6 and 2 Peter 2:4 speak of angels that sinned, and are read by some as referring to this passage; neither mentions Genesis 6, marriage or daughters of men. Matthew 22:30 is cited by others against the first reading; it speaks of the resurrection and of angels in heaven and does not mention Genesis 6 either. Check made for an answer elsewhere: the packaged KJV was searched for “sons of God” (11 verses: Genesis 6:2, 6:4; Job 1:6, 2:1, 38:7; John 1:12; Romans 8:14, 8:19; Philippians 2:15; 1 John 3:1, 3:2) and all were read; Matthew 22:30, Jude 1:6–7 and 2 Peter 2:4–5 were read as well. None says who the sons of God of Genesis 6 were. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible, and it does not prove that no passage addresses the question. No G tag is proposed: in Genesis 6:2 and 6:4 Brenton’s Greek agrees with the KJV. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. title: Why was Canaan cursed for what Ham did?
summary: Ham sees his father’s nakedness and tells his brothers. When Noah wakes, he curses not Ham but Ham’s son Canaan. The passage does not say why the curse falls on Canaan, or what was “done unto” Noah beyond the seeing and telling.
text: KJV Genesis 9:18: “and Ham is the father of Canaan”. KJV 9:22: “And Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father, and told his two brethren without.” Hebrew (WLC) 9:22: וַיַּ֗רְא חָ֚ם אֲבִ֣י כְנַ֔עַן אֵ֖ת עֶרְוַ֣ת אָבִ֑יו [and Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 9:22: Καὶ εἶδε Χὰμ ὁ πατὴρ Χαναὰν τὴν γύμνωσιν τοῦ πατρὸς αὐτοῦ [and Ham, the father of Canaan, saw the nakedness of his father]. KJV 9:24: “And Noah awoke from his wine, and knew what his younger son had done unto him.” Hebrew (WLC) 9:24: וַיֵּ֕דַע אֵ֛ת אֲשֶׁר־עָ֥שָׂה־לֹ֖ו בְּנֹ֥ו הַקָּטָֽן [and he knew what his son, the young one, had done to him]. Brenton Greek 9:24: καὶ ἔγνω ὅσα ἐποίησεν αὐτῷ ὁ υἱὸς αὐτοῦ ὁ νεώτερος [and he knew all that his younger son had done to him]. KJV 9:25: “And he said, Cursed be Canaan; a servant of servants shall he be unto his brethren.” Hebrew (WLC) 9:25: אָר֣וּר כְּנָ֑עַן [cursed be Canaan]. Brenton Greek 9:25: ἐπικατάρατος Χαναὰν [cursed be Canaan]. KJV 9:26: “and Canaan shall be his servant”. KJV 9:27: “and Canaan shall be his servant”. KJV 10:6: “And the sons of Ham; Cush, and Mizraim, and Phut, and Canaan.” KJV 5:32: “Noah begat Shem, Ham, and Japheth”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/9/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN09.htm.
reasoning: The only act the passage reports of Ham is that he saw his father’s nakedness and told his two brothers. Verse 24 then speaks of something “done unto” Noah. The curse that follows names Canaan three times and does not name Ham. Canaan has done nothing in the story as told; he is mentioned only as Ham’s son, and Ham has three other sons (10:6) who are not cursed. The passage gives no reason for the curse falling on the son, and does not say whether “done” means more than the seeing and telling. Verse 24 calls the doer Noah’s “younger son”, while each list of the three sons puts Ham second (5:32; 9:18); the passage does not explain that either.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readers have proposed that Canaan took part in the act, that a father is punished through his son, that more was done than the passage reports, or that Noah would not curse a son whom God had blessed in 9:1. Each is an interpretation; the passage states none of them, and this record asserts none. The order of names in a list does not by itself prove order of birth, so the “younger son” wording is noted and not pressed. Check made for an answer elsewhere: every verse of the packaged KJV outside Genesis that contains the name Ham was read (1 Chronicles 1:4, 1:8, 4:40; Psalms 78:51, 105:23, 105:27, 106:22), and the packaged KJV was searched for verses containing both “Canaan” and a form of “curse” (Genesis 9:25 only). None gives a reason for the curse on Canaan. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible, and it does not prove that no passage addresses the question. title: Whom does God address as “us”?
summary: Three times in Genesis God speaks in the plural: “Let us make man”, “as one of us”, “let us go down”. The narrative on either side speaks of God acting in the singular. The passages do not say who is addressed.
text: KJV Genesis 1:26: “And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness”. Hebrew (WLC) 1:26: נַֽעֲשֶׂ֥ה אָדָ֛ם בְּצַלְמֵ֖נוּ כִּדְמוּתֵ֑נוּ [let us make man in our image, according to our likeness]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 1:26: Ποιήσωμεν ἄνθρωπον κατʼ εἰκόνα ἡμετέραν καὶ καθʼ ὁμοίωσιν [let us make man according to our image and according to likeness]. KJV 1:27: “So God created man in his own image”. KJV 3:22: “And the Lord God said, Behold, the man is become as one of us, to know good and evil”. Hebrew (WLC) 3:22: הֵ֤ן הָֽאָדָם֙ הָיָה֙ כְּאַחַ֣ד מִמֶּ֔נּוּ [behold, the man has become like one of us]. Brenton Greek 3:22: ἰδοὺ Ἀδὰμ γέγονεν ὡς εἷς ἐξ ἡμῶν [behold, Adam has become as one of us]. KJV 11:5: “And the Lord came down to see the city and the tower”. KJV 11:7: “Go to, let us go down, and there confound their language”. Hebrew (WLC) 11:7: הָ֚בָה נֵֽרְדָ֔ה וְנָבְלָ֥ה שָׁ֖ם שְׂפָתָ֑ם [come, let us go down and confuse their language there]. Brenton Greek 11:7: Δεῦτε, καὶ καταβάντες συγχέωμεν αὐτῶν ἐκεῖ τὴν γλῶσσαν [come, and having gone down let us confound their tongue there]. KJV 11:8: “So the Lord scattered them abroad”. KJV Isaiah 6:8: “Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?” KJV 1 Kings 22:19: “I saw the Lord sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing by him”. KJV Job 38:7: “and all the sons of God shouted for joy”. KJV Isaiah 40:14: “With whom took he counsel”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/1/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN01.htm; https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/3/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN03.htm; https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/11/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN11.htm.
reasoning: In each of the three places the speaker is God and the words are plural: “us” and “our”. The plural is in the Hebrew and in Brenton’s Greek as well as in the KJV. In each place the act itself is then told in the singular: God created man in his own image (1:27); the Lord came down (11:5) and the Lord scattered them (11:8). None of the three passages names anyone else as present, and none says to whom the words are spoken.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readers have taken the plural as God addressing heavenly beings around him, as a way of speaking of himself, or as a plurality within God. Each is an interpretation; Genesis states none of them, and this record asserts none. Isaiah 6:8 has the same kind of plural in the Lord’s own speech; 1 Kings 22:19 and Job 38:7 speak of heavenly beings in God’s presence; Isaiah 40:14 asks with whom he took counsel. None of these mentions the Genesis passages or says who is addressed there. Check made for an answer elsewhere: only the passages quoted here were read (Isaiah 6:8; 1 Kings 22:19–20; Job 38:7; Isaiah 40:13–14). A pronoun cannot usefully be word-searched, so no search of the whole packaged KJV was made, and nothing is claimed about the rest of the Bible. title: Who was Melchizedek, and how did he come to be priest of the most high God?
summary: Melchizedek appears for three verses as king of Salem and priest of the most high God, blesses Abram and receives a tenth, and is not mentioned again in Genesis. His people, his descent and how he came to be a priest are not stated.
text: KJV Genesis 14:18: “And Melchizedek king of Salem brought forth bread and wine: and he was the priest of the most high God.” Hebrew (WLC) 14:18: וּמַלְכִּי־צֶ֙דֶק֙ מֶ֣לֶךְ שָׁלֵ֔ם הֹוצִ֖יא לֶ֣חֶם וָיָ֑יִן וְה֥וּא כֹהֵ֖ן לְאֵ֥ל עֶלְיֹֽון [and Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine; and he was priest to God Most High]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 14:18: ἦν δὲ ἱερεὺς τοῦ Θεοῦ τοῦ ὑψίστου [and he was priest of God the Most High]. KJV 14:19: “Blessed be Abram of the most high God, possessor of heaven and earth”. KJV 14:20: “And he gave him tithes of all.” KJV 14:22: “I have lift up mine hand unto the Lord, the most high God, the possessor of heaven and earth”. KJV Psalms 110:4: “Thou art a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek.” KJV Psalms 76:2: “In Salem also is his tabernacle, and his dwelling place in Zion.” KJV Hebrews 7:1: “For this Melchisedec, king of Salem, priest of the most high God, who met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings, and blessed him”. KJV Hebrews 7:3: “Without father, without mother, without descent, having neither beginning of days, nor end of life; but made like unto the Son of God; abideth a priest continually.” Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/14/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN14.htm.
reasoning: Genesis 14:18 is the first verse in the packaged KJV that contains the word “priest”. Melchizedek is introduced without parents, people or history; he is a king of a city in the land where Abram is a stranger, and he is priest of the God whom Abram in verse 22 names as the Lord. Abram accepts his blessing and a tenth is given. The passage does not say how a king of Salem came to serve that God, who made him a priest, or what became of him.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is taken up elsewhere but, on the check made, not answered. Hebrews 7:3 remarks on exactly this: “Without father, without mother, without descent”. Readers take that either as a statement about the man himself or as a statement about what the record leaves out; Hebrews does not say which, and it gives him no people or lineage. Psalms 110:4 speaks of an “order of Melchizedek” without describing how it began. That Salem is Jerusalem is drawn by readers from Psalms 76:2; Genesis does not say so. That he was a human priest-king, or an appearance of a heavenly figure, are both interpretations; the passage states neither, and this record asserts neither. Check made for an answer elsewhere: every verse of the packaged KJV containing “Melchizedek” or “Melchisedec” was read (11 verses: Genesis 14:18; Psalms 110:4; Hebrews 5:6, 5:10, 6:20, 7:1, 7:10, 7:11, 7:15, 7:17, 7:21), with Hebrews 7:2–4. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible, and it does not prove that no passage addresses the question. No G tag is proposed: in 14:18 Brenton’s Greek agrees with the KJV. title: Is the angel of the Lord a messenger, or the Lord himself?
summary: In Genesis the angel of the Lord speaks in the first person as God: “I will multiply thy seed”, “thou hast not withheld thy son … from me”, “I am the God of Bethel”. Hagar names “the Lord that spake unto her”. The passages do not say whether the angel is someone other than God or God himself appearing.
text: KJV Genesis 16:10: “And the angel of the Lord said unto her, I will multiply thy seed exceedingly, that it shall not be numbered for multitude.” Hebrew (WLC) 16:10: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לָהּ֙ מַלְאַ֣ךְ יְהוָ֔ה הַרְבָּ֥ה אַרְבֶּ֖ה אֶת־זַרְעֵ֑ךְ [and the angel of YHWH said to her, I will greatly multiply your seed]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 16:10: Καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῇ ὁ ἄγγελος Κυρίου, πληθύνων πληθυνῶ τὸ σπέρμα σου [and the angel of the Lord said to her, multiplying I will multiply your seed]. KJV 16:11: “because the Lord hath heard thy affliction”. KJV 16:13: “And she called the name of the Lord that spake unto her, Thou God seest me”. Hebrew (WLC) 16:13: וַתִּקְרָ֤א שֵׁם־יְהוָה֙ הַדֹּבֵ֣ר אֵלֶ֔יהָ [and she called the name of YHWH who was speaking to her]. Brenton Greek 16:13: Καὶ ἐκάλεσε τὸ ὄνομα Κυρίου τοῦ λαλοῦντος πρὸς αὐτὴν [and she called the name of the Lord who was speaking to her]. KJV 22:11: “And the angel of the Lord called unto him out of heaven”. KJV 22:12: “for now I know that thou fearest God, seeing thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son from me”. Hebrew (WLC) 22:12: וְלֹ֥א חָשַׂ֛כְתָּ אֶת־בִּנְךָ֥ אֶת־יְחִידְךָ֖ מִמֶּֽנִּי [and you have not withheld your son, your only one, from me]. KJV 22:15: “And the angel of the Lord called unto Abraham out of heaven the second time,” KJV 22:16: “And said, By myself have I sworn, saith the Lord”. KJV 31:11: “And the angel of God spake unto me in a dream”. Hebrew (WLC) 31:11: וַיֹּ֨אמֶר אֵלַ֜י מַלְאַ֧ךְ הָאֱלֹהִ֛ים בַּחֲלֹ֖ום [and the angel of God said to me in the dream]. KJV 31:13: “I am the God of Bethel, where thou anointedst the pillar, and where thou vowedst a vow unto me”. Hebrew (WLC) 31:13: אָנֹכִ֤י הָאֵל֙ בֵּֽית־אֵ֔ל [I am the God of Bethel]. Brenton Greek 31:13: Ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ Θεὸς ὁ ὀφθείς σοι ἐν τόπῳ Θεοῦ [I am the God who appeared to you in the place of God]. KJV Exodus 3:2: “And the angel of the Lord appeared unto him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush”. KJV Exodus 3:4: “God called unto him out of the midst of the bush”. KJV Judges 13:21: “Then Manoah knew that he was an angel of the Lord.” KJV Judges 13:22: “We shall surely die, because we have seen God.” KJV Zechariah 1:12: “Then the angel of the Lord answered and said, O Lord of hosts, how long wilt thou not have mercy on Jerusalem”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/16/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN16.htm; https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/22/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN22.htm; https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/31/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN31.htm.
reasoning: The narrator calls the speaker “the angel of the Lord” or “the angel of God”. The speaker then says things in the first person that belong to God: he will multiply Hagar’s seed; Abraham has not withheld his son “from me”; “I am the God of Bethel”. In the same speeches he also speaks of God as another: “the Lord hath heard thy affliction” (16:11), “thou fearest God” (22:12). Hagar’s response is to name “the Lord that spake unto her”. At 22:16 the words are marked as a message, “saith the Lord”; at 16:10 and 31:13 there is no such mark. The passages do not say whether the angel is a being sent by God who speaks God’s words, or God appearing.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readers have taken the angel as a messenger who speaks his sender’s words in the first person, as an appearance of God himself, or as a distinct divine person. Each is an interpretation; the passages state none of them, and this record asserts none. The same alternation is found outside Genesis: at the bush the angel of the Lord appears and God calls (Exodus 3:2, 3:4), and Manoah, knowing he had seen an angel of the Lord, says they have seen God (Judges 13:21–22). In Zechariah 1:12 the angel of the Lord addresses the Lord of hosts as another. These show the question recurs; they do not settle it for Genesis. None says what the angel of the Lord is. That is a word search with a partial reading, not a reading of the whole Bible, and it does not prove that no passage addresses the question. title: Who were the three men at Mamre, and was the Lord one of them?
summary: The Lord appears to Abraham; Abraham looks up and sees three men. Later “the men” leave for Sodom while Abraham still stands before the Lord, and two angels arrive at Sodom. The passage does not say how the Lord and the three men are related, or why three become two.
text: KJV Genesis 18:1: “And the Lord appeared unto him in the plains of Mamre”. Hebrew (WLC) 18:1: וַיֵּרָ֤א אֵלָיו֙ יְהוָ֔ה [and YHWH appeared to him]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 18:1: Ὤφθη δὲ αὐτῷ ὁ Θεὸς [and God appeared to him]. KJV 18:2: “And he lift up his eyes and looked, and, lo, three men stood by him”. Hebrew (WLC) 18:2: וְהִנֵּה֙ שְׁלֹשָׁ֣ה אֲנָשִׁ֔ים נִצָּבִ֖ים עָלָ֑יו [and behold, three men standing by him]. Brenton Greek 18:2: καὶ ἰδοὺ τρεῖς ἄνδρες εἱστήκεισαν ἐπάνω αὐτοῦ [and behold, three men stood over him]. KJV 18:3: “My Lord, if now I have found favour in thy sight”. KJV 18:9: “And they said unto him, Where is Sarah thy wife?” KJV 18:10: “And he said, I will certainly return unto thee”. KJV 18:13: “And the Lord said unto Abraham, Wherefore did Sarah laugh”. KJV 18:22: “And the men turned their faces from thence, and went toward Sodom: but Abraham stood yet before the Lord.” Hebrew (WLC) 18:22: וַיִּפְנ֤וּ מִשָּׁם֙ הָֽאֲנָשִׁ֔ים וַיֵּלְכ֖וּ סְדֹ֑מָה וְאַ֨בְרָהָ֔ם עֹודֶ֥נּוּ עֹמֵ֖ד לִפְנֵ֥י יְהוָֽה [and the men turned from there and went toward Sodom, and Abraham was still standing before YHWH]. Brenton Greek 18:22: Καὶ ἀποστρέψαντες ἐκεῖθεν οἱ ἄνδρες, ἦλθον εἰς Σόδομα· Ἁβραὰμ δὲ ἔτι ἦν ἑστηκὼς ἐναντίον Κυρίου [and the men, having turned away from there, came to Sodom; and Abraham was still standing before the Lord]. KJV 18:33: “And the Lord went his way, as soon as he had left communing with Abraham”. KJV 19:1: “And there came two angels to Sodom at even”. Hebrew (WLC) 19:1: וַ֠יָּבֹאוּ שְׁנֵ֨י הַמַּלְאָכִ֤ים סְדֹ֙מָה֙ בָּעֶ֔רֶב [and the two angels came to Sodom in the evening]. Brenton Greek 19:1: οἱ δύο ἄγγελοι εἰς Σόδομα ἑσπέρας [the two angels, to Sodom, at evening]. KJV 19:13: “and the Lord hath sent us to destroy it”. KJV Hebrews 13:2: “for thereby some have entertained angels unawares”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/18/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN18.htm; https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/19/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN19.htm.
reasoning: Verse 1 says the Lord appeared; verse 2 says that what Abraham saw was three men. Through the meal and the promise the speaker changes without comment: “they said” (18:9), “he said” (18:10), “the Lord said” (18:13). In verse 22 “the men” go toward Sodom while Abraham still stands before the Lord, and in 19:1 two angels reach Sodom, who say the Lord has sent them. The passage does not say whether the Lord was one of the three, whether all three were his messengers, or what became of the third between Mamre and Sodom.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readers have taken the visitors as the Lord with two angels, as three angels through whom the Lord speaks, or as a showing of God as three. Each is an interpretation; the passage states none of them, and this record asserts none. That the two angels of 19:1 are two of the three men of 18:2 is itself an inference from the order of the story, though a natural one; the Hebrew and Brenton’s Greek say “the two angels”. Whether God can be seen at all is a different matter and is not raised here. Hebrews 13:2 is often connected with this meal; it names neither Abraham nor Mamre. Check made for an answer elsewhere: the packaged KJV was searched for “three men” and for “Mamre” (22 verses); none outside Genesis 18 refers to this visit; Hebrews 13:2 was read. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible, and it does not prove that no passage addresses the question. No G tag is proposed: Brenton’s Greek has “God” where the KJV has “the Lord” at 18:1, which names the same person, and otherwise agrees in the verses quoted. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original. English in square brackets is the researcher’s plain rendering, not a KJV quotation and not a lexicon entry.

title: Who or what is “Shiloh” in Jacob’s blessing of Judah?
summary: Jacob says the sceptre shall not depart from Judah “until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be”. The verse does not say who or what Shiloh is. Everywhere else in the KJV Shiloh is a town, and Brenton’s Greek has no name here.
text: KJV Genesis 49:8: “Judah, thou art he whom thy brethren shall praise”. KJV 49:10: “The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor a lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh come; and unto him shall the gathering of the people be.” Hebrew (WLC) 49:10, as the edition prints it with its written and read spellings: עַ֚ד כִּֽי־יָבֹ֣א [שִׁילֹה כ] (שִׁילֹ֔ו ק) וְלֹ֖ו יִקְּהַ֥ת עַמִּֽים [until shiloh comes, and to him the … of peoples; “shiloh” is left untranslated because it is the word in question, and the word before “of peoples” is not glossed]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek) 49:10: ἕως ἐὰν ἔλθῃ τὰ ἀποκείμενα αὐτῷ· καὶ αὐτὸς προσδοκία ἐθνῶν [until there come the things laid up for him; and he is the expectation of nations]. KJV Joshua 18:1: “assembled together at Shiloh, and set up the tabernacle of the congregation there”. KJV Ezekiel 21:27: “until he come whose right it is; and I will give it him”. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/1/49/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/GEN49.htm.
reasoning: The KJV prints Shiloh as a name and goes on “unto him”, so that Shiloh reads as someone who is to come. No person called Shiloh appears anywhere else in the packaged KJV: the word occurs in 30 other verses, from Joshua 18:1 to Jeremiah 41:5, and in each it is a place. Brenton’s Greek has no name at this point but a phrase, “the things laid up for him”. The verse sets a term to Judah’s sceptre, “until”, and does not say who or what marks that term.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. Readers have taken Shiloh as a title of a ruler to come, as the town, or as a phrase meaning something like “that which is his” or “he whose it is”. Each is an interpretation; the verse states none of them, and this record asserts none. Ezekiel 21:27 has wording that some connect with the third reading; it does not mention Shiloh, Judah’s blessing or Genesis. Check made for an answer elsewhere: the packaged KJV was searched for “Shiloh” (31 verses; Joshua 16:6 has the separate name Taanathshiloh) and the list was read in shortened form; all but Genesis 49:10 concern the town (Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings, Psalms 78:60, Jeremiah), and no New Testament verse contains the word. None explains Genesis 49:10. That is a word search, not a reading of the whole Bible, and it does not prove that no passage addresses the question. The written and read spellings printed in the Hebrew edition are given for completeness only and are not the finding. The Greek is quoted because it bears on the question; this record proposes no G tag, and whether the Greek difference qualifies for one has not been examined here. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees; other Hebrew manuscripts were not examined. The Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation tradition of the Old Testament. It is not a critical apparatus and does not show that all Greek witnesses agree or which reading is original.
